_help: Plant profiles for the South Florida Plants page. Every fact should come from a UF/IFAS or similarly authoritative source listed in 'sources'. Set 'featured' to true to show a plant on the Home page (3 recommended). Each plant has a 'photo' (files in src/assets/img/plants/) and a 'photoCredit'; record new photos in docs/image-credits.md.

items.name: Firebush
items.water: Regular water to establish; fairly drought tolerant once established
items.size: About 8–12 ft tall if left unpruned; compact types stay smaller
items.uses: Butterfly and hummingbird gardens, informal hedges, color at the back of a bed
items.care: Fertilize sparingly. Keep lawn grass out of the root zone. Watch new spring growth for aphids.
items.tip: Nurseries also sell a Central American variety with yellow-orange flowers and smooth leaves. For the true native, look for red-orange flowers and slightly fuzzy leaves.

sources.label: UF/IFAS Extension Charlotte County: A firebush of a different color

photo.alt: Clusters of tubular red-orange firebush flowers among glossy green leaves

items.name: Coontie
items.water: Needs water while getting established; drought tolerant afterward
items.size: Low, fern-like mound; mature clumps can spread several feet
items.uses: Foundation plantings, groundcover masses, shady corners, modern and minimal gardens
items.care: Slow growing and rarely needs pruning. Hard to move once large, so plant it where it can stay.
items.tip: Coontie is the only larval host plant for the rare atala butterfly. Its seeds and roots are poisonous, so place it thoughtfully around children and pets.

sources.label: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions: Plant This, Not That
UF/IFAS Extension Broward County: The atala butterfly

photo.alt: Coontie plant with stiff, glossy, fern-like fronds growing in mulch

items.name: Cocoplum
items.water: Little irrigation once established; avoid soggy soil while young
items.size: Coastal forms stay low (about 18–24 in with pruning); inland forms can reach 15–25 ft
items.care: Plant about 3–4 ft apart for a hedge. Not freeze tolerant. Fruit can drop on walkways for a short time.
items.tip: Pick the form to match the job. 'Horizontal' is the low coastal type; the inland type makes a tall screen.

sources.label: UF/IFAS EDIS: Cocoplum identification and uses

photo.alt: Cocoplum branch with rounded leaves and small white flowers

items.name: Seagrape
items.water: Water regularly until established; very drought tolerant afterward
items.size: Grown as a large shrub, hedge or multi-trunk tree
items.uses: Seaside yards, windbreaks, screens, bold-leaf accents
items.care: Prune by hand because of the large leaves. Young trees need early training. Fallen leaves are slow to break down.
items.tip: Highly salt tolerant, which makes it one of the best choices near the coast. Seagrapes growing in dunes are protected; altering them there requires a state permit.

photo.alt: Large round seagrape leaves with red veins and clusters of green fruit

items.name: Muhly grass
items.water: Water until established; drought tolerant afterward
items.size: Clumps about 2–3 ft tall and wide
items.uses: Mass plantings, borders, rain gardens, natural and modern designs
items.care: Space 2–3 ft apart. Tidy or cut back in late winter before new growth starts. Rarely troubled by pests.
items.tip: Clouds of pink flower plumes appear in fall. Plant in groups so the color reads from a distance and moves with the wind.

photo.alt: Muhly grass with clouds of pink flower plumes above fine green blades

items.name: Wild coffee
items.water: Moderate; may wilt in the dry season without extra water
items.size: About 4–10 ft tall and 4–8 ft wide; dwarf forms stay near 2.5 ft
items.uses: Shady beds, informal hedges, under trees, wildlife gardens
items.care: Needs well-drained soil and seldom needs pruning. For hedges, space about 4 ft apart and keep 4 ft from the house.
items.tip: Glossy, deeply veined leaves brighten shady spots. Birds eat the red fruit, but it isn't for people.

photo.alt: Wild coffee shrub with glossy, deeply veined green leaves

items.name: Simpson's stopper
items.water: Drought tolerant once established; monitor young plants in dry spells
items.size: Shrub or small tree, often 15–20 ft; 'Compacta' stays near 5 ft
items.uses: Hedges, small specimen trees, coastal and wildlife gardens
items.care: Handles shearing well, though heavy pruning reduces flowers and berries. Tolerates salt and alkaline soil.
items.tip: Fragrant white spring flowers, orange-red berries for birds, and peeling cinnamon-colored bark. Buy nursery-grown plants only.

photo.alt: Simpson's stopper branches with small, dense, glossy leaves

items.name: Sabal palm (cabbage palm)
items.water: Keep the root ball moist, not soggy, while establishing; tough afterward
items.uses: Focal points, natural Florida and coastal landscapes
items.care: Plant at the same depth it grew before. Remove only fully dead fronds and avoid 'hurricane cuts', which weaken palms.
items.tip: Tolerates salt spray on its fronds better than salty soil. Seedlings can pop up beneath it, so plan for occasional weeding.

photo.alt: Close view of a sabal palm's fan-shaped frond

items.name: Croton
items.light: Bright light or shifting sun; harsh sun can scorch or fade leaves
items.water: Well-drained soil; let it dry slightly between waterings
items.size: Can reach about 6 ft tall and wide in the ground
items.uses: Color accents, tropical beds, containers, entryways
items.care: Space 2–3 ft apart. Frost damages leaves, but plants usually recover. Occasionally gets scale or mites.
items.tip: Leaves and sap are irritating and poisonous if chewed, and the sap can stain. Wear gloves and keep away from pets that nibble plants.

sources.label: UF/IFAS Extension Polk County: Growing crotons
